lawful-basis.ground.says: Processing is lawful only if one of six listed grounds applies: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
lawful-basis.ground.quote: Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies

lawful-basis.legitimate-interests.says: Yes. Legitimate interests of the controller or a third party are a listed ground, but they yield where the person's interests or rights override them. Public authorities cannot use it for their tasks.
lawful-basis.legitimate-interests.quote: processing is necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party

consent.standard.says: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and given by a statement or a clear affirmative action. Consent must be shown, not assumed.
consent.standard.quote: any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes

consent.role.says: Consent is one of six legal grounds for processing, with no priority over the others. The controller may rely on contract, legal obligation, legitimate interests or another listed ground instead.
consent.role.quote: the data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes

consent.withdrawal.says: Yes, at any time. Withdrawal does not make earlier processing unlawful, the person must be told of this before consenting, and withdrawing must be as easy as giving consent.
consent.withdrawal.quote: The data subject shall have the right to withdraw his or her consent at any time

consent.separate.says: Explicit consent is required for special-category data (Art. 9(2)(a)). Explicit consent is also an exception for solely automated decisions (Art. 22(2)(c)) and, as a fallback, for transfers abroad (Art. 49(1)(a)).
consent.separate.quote: the data subject has given explicit consent to the processing of those personal data for one or more specified purposes

notice.timing.says: Yes. Where data come from the person, the notice is due at the time the data are obtained. Where they come from another source, it is due within a reasonable period and at the latest within one month.
notice.timing.quote: the controller shall, at the time when personal data are obtained, provide the data subject with all of the following information

notice.content.says: A long prescribed list: controller identity and contact details, purposes and legal basis, recipients, transfers abroad, storage period, the person's rights, the right to complain, and whether automated decisions are made.
notice.content.quote: the period for which the personal data will be stored, or if that is not possible, the criteria used to determine that period

access.right.says: The person can get confirmation that data are processed, a copy of the data, and details: purposes, categories, recipients, storage period, sources, and the logic of any automated decisions.
access.right.ownTerm: right of access by the data subject
access.right.quote: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning him or her are being processed

access.deadline.says: Without undue delay and in any event within one month of the request. The controller may extend this by two further months for complex or numerous requests, if it tells the person within the first month.
access.deadline.quote: and in any event within one month of receipt of the request

deletion.right.says: Yes. The person can require erasure without undue delay where a listed ground applies, such as data no longer being needed, consent being withdrawn, or unlawful processing. Exceptions apply under Art. 17(3).
deletion.right.quote: the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay

deletion.pass-on.says: Yes. Where the controller has made data public and must erase it, it must take reasonable steps to tell other controllers processing the data to erase links, copies or replications. Art. 19 also requires notifying recipients.
deletion.pass-on.quote: shall take reasonable steps, including technical measures, to inform controllers which are processing the personal data

correction.right.says: Yes. The person can obtain rectification of inaccurate personal data without undue delay, and can have incomplete data completed, including by a supplementary statement.
correction.right.quote: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate personal data concerning him or her

correction.pass-on.says: Yes. Any rectification, erasure or restriction must be communicated to each recipient the data were disclosed to, unless this is impossible or involves disproportionate effort. The person can ask who those recipients are.
correction.pass-on.quote: The controller shall communicate any rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing

portability.right.says: They can receive the data they provided in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, and can have it sent directly to another controller where technically feasible. Applies to consent or contract based, automated processing.
portability.right.quote: the data subject shall have the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible

optout.marketing.says: They can object at any time to processing for direct marketing, including profiling linked to it. Once they object, the data must no longer be used for marketing. The right must be brought to their attention at first contact.
optout.marketing.quote: the data subject shall have the right to object at any time to processing of personal data concerning him or her for such marketing

optout.sale.says: The GDPR has no rule about sale as such. Passing data to others is processing and needs a lawful ground under Art. 6, such as consent or legitimate interests. Some uses can also be stopped by objection (Art. 21).
optout.sale.quote: Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies

adm.protection.says: They have the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, unless an exception applies. Where an exception applies, they can obtain human intervention and contest the decision.
adm.protection.quote: The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling

sensitive.category.says: Yes. Art. 9(1) lists a fixed set of special categories: racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic and biometric data, health, and sex life or orientation.
sensitive.category.quote: Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership

sensitive.rule.says: Processing special-category data is prohibited unless one of the listed exceptions in Art. 9(2) applies, such as explicit consent, employment or social security law, health care, or substantial public interest.
sensitive.rule.quote: Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies

children.rule.says: For information society services offered directly to a child, processing is lawful from age 16. Below 16, a parent or guardian must give or authorise consent. Member States may lower the age, but not below 13.
children.rule.quote: the processing of the personal data of a child shall be lawful where the child is at least 16 years old

breach.regulator.says: Yes, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of the breach, unless it is unlikely to risk people's rights and freedoms. Late notice must give reasons for the delay.
breach.regulator.quote: not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority

breach.individuals.says: Yes, without undue delay, when the breach is likely to result in a high risk to people's rights and freedoms. Notice is not needed if the data are unintelligible (for example encrypted) or the high risk is no longer likely.
breach.individuals.quote: the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject without undue delay

breach.records.says: Yes. The controller must document every personal data breach: the facts, its effects and the remedial action taken, so that the supervisory authority can verify compliance.
breach.records.quote: The controller shall document any personal data breaches, comprising the facts relating to the personal data breach, its effects and the remedial action taken

dpo.officer.says: Only in listed cases: where processing is by a public authority, or where core activities involve large-scale regular and systematic monitoring or large-scale processing of sensitive or criminal-conviction data. Otherwise it is optional.
dpo.officer.quote: The controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer in any case where

dpo.local-representative.says: Yes, where Art. 3(2) applies (offering goods or services to people in the EU, or monitoring them there). Exempt: occasional low-risk processing, and public bodies. The representative must be in the Union.
dpo.local-representative.quote: Where Article 3(2) applies, the controller or the processor shall designate in writing a representative in the Union

dpia.duty.says: Yes, before processing likely to be high risk. Art. 35(3) lists cases: large-scale evaluation with significant effects, large-scale sensitive or criminal data, and large-scale public monitoring. Authorities publish further lists.
dpia.duty.quote: the controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data

dpia.regulator.says: Yes, in some cases. Where the assessment shows a high risk that the controller cannot mitigate, it must consult the supervisory authority before processing (Art. 36). The authority may then give written advice or use its powers.
dpia.regulator.quote: The controller shall consult the supervisory authority prior to processing where a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 indicates that the processing would result in a high risk

transfer.rule.says: Transfers outside the EU need an adequacy decision, or appropriate safeguards such as standard clauses or binding corporate rules (Arts. 45-46). Narrow derogations exist (Art. 49). No risk assessment is named.
transfer.rule.quote: a controller or processor may transfer personal data to a third country or an international organisation only if the controller or processor has provided appropriate safeguards

transfer.tell-people.says: They must be told, at collection or within a reasonable period and at the latest one month later, that the controller intends to transfer data to a third country, and whether an adequacy decision or safeguards apply.
transfer.tell-people.quote: the controller intends to transfer personal data to a third country or international organisation

localization.rule.says: No. The GDPR does not require personal data to be stored in the EU. It regulates transfers out of the EU instead, in Chapter V (Arts. 44-49).
localization.rule.quote: Any transfer of personal data which are undergoing processing or are intended for processing after transfer to a third country

records.duty.says: Controllers must keep a written record of each processing activity: purposes, data subjects and data categories, recipients, transfers abroad, erasure time limits and security measures. Processors keep a similar record.
records.duty.quote: shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility

vendor.contract.says: A processor must be bound by a contract setting out subject-matter, duration, purpose and data types, with listed terms: instructions only, confidentiality, security, sub-processor limits, and deletion or return.
vendor.contract.quote: Processing by a processor shall be governed by a contract or other legal act under Union or Member State law

vendor.direct-duties.says: Yes. Processors must keep records (Art. 30(2)), apply security measures (Art. 32), and notify breaches to the controller (Art. 33(2)). A processor is liable for damage where it breaches duties directed at processors (Art. 82(2)).
vendor.direct-duties.quote: A processor shall be liable for the damage caused by processing only where it has not complied with obligations of this Regulation specifically directed to processors

security.duty.says: The controller and processor must apply appropriate technical and organisational measures for the risk. The text names pseudonymisation and encryption, confidentiality and resilience, restoring access, and regular testing.
security.duty.quote: the controller and the processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk

enforcement.fines.says: Yes. Supervisory authorities can fine up to EUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for the most serious breaches. Other breaches face up to EUR 10 million or 2% (Art. 83(4)).
enforcement.fines.quote: up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher

enforcement.private-action.says: Yes. Anyone who suffers material or non-material damage from an infringement can claim compensation from the controller or processor (Art. 82(1)), and can bring court proceedings against them (Art. 79).
enforcement.private-action.quote: shall have the right to receive compensation from the controller or processor for the damage suffered

organisation.quote: ‘controller’ means the natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data

vendor.quote: ‘processor’ means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which processes personal data on behalf of the controller

person.quote: any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’)

data.quote: ‘personal data’ means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person

sensitive.quote: Processing of special categories of personal data

regulator.quote: ‘supervisory authority’ means an independent public authority which is established by a Member State pursuant to Article 51
